query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is primarily governed by interfacial dislocation nucleation and accumulation driven by lattice distortion and compositional complexity. The interfaces act as both barriers and sources for dislocations, so that variations in interface coherence can modulate the overall creep response.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy phases with coherent interfaces and controlled grain boundary morphology.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the interface coherence (e.g., by altering deposition parameters or post-deposition heat treatments) without changing the overall bulk composition.
generation.conditions: Sustained high-temperature and mechanical loading conditions (creep testing conditions) where dislocation-mediated creep is expected to be dominant, and with layer thicknesses maintained in the nanoscale regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Interfacial regions between the FCC and BCC layers; these zones, marked by severe lattice distortion and compositional complexities, govern dislocation nucleation and accumulation.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load, the lattice mismatch and compositional variations at the interfaces promote dislocation nucleation. As dislocations accumulate at the coherent interfaces, they interact and lead to progressive plastic deformation. Improved interface coherence reduces dislocation nucleation while degraded interfaces promote higher dislocation activity, thus controlling the creep behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with enhanced interface coherence will exhibit lower dislocation nucleation rates and slower creep strain rates compared to a baseline multilayer with standard deposition. Conversely, samples with intentionally diffused or less coherent interfaces will display accelerated plastic deformation due to increased dislocation activity at the interfaces.
generation.baseline: The standard nanoscale multilayer with well-defined FCC/BCC interfaces prepared under conventional deposition conditions, exhibiting a moderate creep rate under sustained loading.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the multilayer thickness remains in the nanoscale regime (to maintain interface-dominated behavior) and within a temperature range where dislocation creep is the primary deformation mechanism. Deviations outside these boundaries (e.g., thicker layers or temperatures promoting diffusion-dominated creep) may not follow the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The interplay between the effects of interface coherence and other microstructural features (such as grain boundary serration observed in SLM HEAs) is not fully understood, which may alter the relative contributions of dislocation mechanisms in multilayer systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayer samples with identical bulk composition but with systematically varied interface coherence (controlled through modifications in deposition parameters or post-treatment heat processes). Subject all samples to identical sustained high-temperature and mechanical loading (creep) tests.
measurements: Creep strain rate via long-term mechanical loading tests
Dislocation density and distribution at interfaces using transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Interface coherence and width determination using atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM
Nanoindentation to assess local mechanical properties at the interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with improved interface coherence do not show reduced dislocation nucleation rates and slower creep rates compared to the baseline, or if degraded interface samples fail to show accelerated plastic deformation, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

AbstractHigh-temperature creep refers to the slow and continuous plastic deformation of materials under the effects of high temperatures and mechanical stress over extended periods, which can lead to the degradation or even failure of the components’ functionality. AlxCr0.2NbTiV (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) refractory high-entropy alloys were fabricated by arc melting. The effects of Al content on the microstructure of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were studied using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction. The microhardness, compression properties, and nanoindentation creep properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were also tested. ## Abstract
AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Additionally, the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction are found to critically affect the alloy’s creep resistance. ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively.
